concept: auxiliary vs lexical verbs: not and inversion
statement: Auxiliary verbs can be negated by a following 'not' and can invert with the subject in interrogatives; lexical verbs cannot, and need the dummy auxiliary do instead.
condition: Applies to a clause whose verb is a lexical (non-auxiliary) verb in a construction requiring negation with 'not' or subject-verb inversion: the lexical verb cannot itself be followed by 'not' or placed before the subject; the dummy auxiliary 'do' must be inserted.
violation: A lexical (non-auxiliary) verb is directly followed by 'not', or is placed before its subject to form an interrogative, without 'do' or another auxiliary.

correct.text: Do you want to go with them?

incorrect.note: Lexical verb 'saw' followed directly by 'not'. Source pattern: p. 51 [3i].
Lexical verb inverted with subject. Source pattern: p. 51 [3ii].

review_notes: Described for contemporary standard English; the page does not mention archaic or poetic uses ('I know not'). 'Be' counts as an auxiliary even as copula (WCAT-002), so it is not subject to this restriction.

concept: be as auxiliary in copula use
statement: Because auxiliaries are defined syntactically, be is an auxiliary verb even in its copula use, as in 'They are cheap', where it takes 'not' and inverts with the subject.
condition: Applies to the verb be in any use (progressive, passive or copula): it takes a following 'not' and inverts with the subject to form interrogatives.

statement: Mood is a matter of grammatical form and modality of meaning; the main markers of mood in English are the modal auxiliaries can, may, must, will, shall (plus a few less central ones), and irrealis were is a residual mood form.
condition: Applies when identifying modal auxiliaries: can, may, must, will and shall are central modals; modality (meaning) can be expressed by means other than modals.

correct.text: I wish he were here. [irrealis mood]

statement: Prototypical NPs are headed by nouns and can function as complement; the main noun subcategories are common nouns, proper nouns and pronouns, and pronoun is a subcategory of noun, not a distinct part of speech.
condition: Applies when classifying words heading NPs: common noun, proper noun and pronoun are all subcategories of noun.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge departs from the traditional part-of-speech list; Burton-Roberts's treatment not checked.

traditional_terms: pronoun as a part of speech

statement: Determiner is a function in NP structure and determinative is a lexical category; determinatives are a distinct primary category (traditionally a subclass of adjectives) and can have functions other than determiner, while determiners may also be genitive NPs.
condition: Applies to words like the, a, my, three, much: determinative is the category and determiner the NP-internal function marking definiteness; a determinative may instead function as modifier (e.g. in 'these three books'), and a genitive NP may be the determiner.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge's 'determinative' category contradicts the traditional treatment; compare with Burton-Roberts.

review_notes: Flag for Burton-Roberts comparison: category inventory differs from traditional grammar.

statement: Noun senses are either count (a dog; combine with cardinal numerals) or non-count (some equipment); certain determiners occur only or almost only with count nouns (a, each, every, either, several, many) and others with non-count nouns (much, little, a little).
condition: Applies to the sense of a noun in context: a count sense can combine with one, two, three; a non-count sense cannot; determiner selection follows the count/non-count distinction.

review_notes: The book hedges ('only, or almost only'); this is descriptive and not an error rule. Classification is by noun sense, not by word.

statement: Adjectives have two major uses, attributive modifier in NP structure and predicative complement in clause structure; most adjectives occur in both, and adjectives can also be postpositive (post-head modifier).
condition: Applies to adjective use: attributive = before the noun inside an NP; predicative = complement of a verb such as be; postpositive = after the head noun (something unusual, the money available).

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: Some adjectives (in some senses) are restricted to attributive function and a few cannot be used attributively, so function must be checked word by word.
condition: Applies to individual adjectives: an attributive-only adjective such as 'sole' cannot be a predicative complement, and an adjective such as 'asleep' cannot be an attributive modifier.
violation: An attributive-only adjective (e.g. sole) is used as predicative complement, or a non-attributive adjective (e.g. asleep) is used before a noun.

exceptions.description: The attributive-only restriction can hold only 'in a given sense' of an adjective, not for every sense; most adjectives occur in both functions.

review_notes: Lexical restriction: only the words the book names (sole, asleep) are supported here. The full lists need Ch. 6. Do not generalise to other adjectives.

statement: Unlike adjectives, adverbs do not occur as predicative complement.
condition: Applies to the predicative complement position (as after be): an adjective may fill it, a (-ly) adverb may not.
violation: An adverb (e.g. a form in -ly) is used as predicative complement.

review_notes: Stated generally on p. 57; Cambridge's treatment of words like 'there' or 'well' in this position is not given here, so exclude them from engine checks until Ch. 6 is processed.

statement: Adverbs generally function as modifiers (or supplements); adjectives modify nominals whereas adverbs modify other categories, including verbs, adjectives, adverbs and NPs, though not every adverb can modify every category.
condition: Applies to modification: nominal heads take adjective modifiers; verbs, adjectives, adverbs and NPs take adverb modifiers; supplements are adverbs detached prosodically from the clause.

correct.text: They ate almost the whole cake. [modifies NP]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: 'Not all adverbs can modify heads of all these categories' (p. 57); the engine must not assume 'almost'-style freedom for every adverb.

statement: Adverb is the least homogeneous traditional part of speech; many adverbs are formed from adjectives by adding -ly, and Cambridge reduces the heterogeneity by moving many traditional adverbs into the preposition category.
condition: Applies when classifying adverbs: -ly derivation links many adverbs to adjectives (excellent ~ excellently); the adverb/preposition boundary is redrawn so that words like 'before' and 'afterwards' count as prepositions.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge narrows the adverb class; Burton-Roberts's boundary not checked.

review_notes: Includes the §6 statement that only a very small number of adverbs license complements (independently of such considerations).

statement: Prepositions are heads of preposition phrases, and words like before, until, afterwards are prepositions whether their complement is an NP, a clause, an adverb phrase, or absent; many traditional adverbs and most traditional subordinating conjunctions are therefore prepositions here.
condition: Applies when classifying words like before, after, until, if, because: if the word heads a phrase with a complement (NP, AdvP, clause) or none, it is a preposition.

correct.text: I saw him before lunch. [NP complement]
I saw him before he left. [clause complement]
I hadn't seen him before. [no complement]
I saw him afterwards. [never takes a complement]
I haven't met him until recently. [AdvP complement]
It depends on how much they cost. [clause complement]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: A major departure from traditional grammar; compare Burton-Roberts's treatment of 'before', 'if', 'because'.

review_notes: Flag for Burton-Roberts comparison: category boundaries differ.

statement: 'More' is the inflectional comparative form of the determinative 'many' and also an adverb in analytic comparatives like 'more expensive'; 'less' is the comparative of determinative 'little' and also an adverb.
condition: Applies to more and less: determinative 'more' = comparative of many (more plays); adverb 'more' marks an analytic comparative; 'less' is likewise a determinative form and an adverb.

correct.text: She wrote more plays than he did. [determinative]
It was more expensive. [adverb, analytic comparative]
I have less patience than you. [determinative]
It was less painful than I'd expected. [adverb]

statement: Certain determinatives, pre-head adjective phrases, and relative clauses occur exclusively or almost exclusively with nouns as head.
condition: When a noun heads an NP or nominal, its dependent set may include noun-associated determinatives, pre-head AdjPs, and relative clauses, which occur exclusively or almost exclusively with nouns as head.

contrast.text: bright lanterns [pre-head AdjP with noun head]
lanterns that glow [relative clause with noun head]

statement: A noun does not take a direct object, unlike a verb; nominal dependents that express related content are not direct objects of the noun.
condition: When a noun functions as the head of a nominal, it cannot be followed by an NP functioning as its direct object; a related dependent may instead occur in a construction licensed by the noun, such as a PP.
violation: A noun head is analysed as taking a bare NP direct object, as though it were a transitive verb.

correct.note: The verb takes the direct object NP.

correct.text: The students’ criticism of the decision was clear.
correct.note: The noun is followed by a PP, not a direct object.
The verb takes the direct object NP.

correct.text: The guide’s description of the route was accurate.
correct.note: The noun is followed by a PP, not a direct object.

incorrect.text: *The students’ criticism the decision was clear.
*The guide’s description the route was accurate.
